study: Meng, Wang, Yang & Zhang, Education Competition and Fertility Intention: Evidence from China's Private Tutoring Ban
policy_or_shock: 2021 ban on for-profit academic tutoring; intensity = per-capita tutoring institutions in 2016, five years pre-policy, from firm registrations
design: (a) survey experiment eliciting fertility intentions with/without policy, within-subject with individual FE plus a between-subject arm; (b) city-level DID on ACTUAL birth rates, 2016-19 avg and 2020 Census vs 2023 (319 cities) and 2024 (204), city+year FE, controls lagged GDPpc/housing price/public ed spend/COVID, SE clustered by city
return_separated: YES - a tutoring ban does not change the RETURN to human capital, only the investment needed to hold a rank; the authors' decomposition separates perceived competition from money and time cost
own_income_held: YES - individual FE; city FE and lagged GDPpc in the DID
outcome: expected total fertility (stated); city birth rate per 1,000 (realized)
effect: +7-8% expected total fertility, larger where intensity higher; DID: higher-intensity cities had significantly greater increases in ACTUAL births. Decomposition: perceived reduction in educational competition is the PRIMARY driver, then parental health (>0.5 SD), then time (-0.69 h/day) and money (-275 RMB/mo, -34.5%)
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS - and the competition channel dominates the pure cost channel
routing: C.2.f's own. The money/time sub-channel is C.2.b's and is reported separately, so the two are separable rather than jointly claimed.

study: Kim, The impact of shadow education expenditures on fertility rates in South Korea
policy_or_shock: none - instrumented variation in provincial shadow-education spending
design: fixed-effects IV. Instrument: changes in the provincial composition of parents WITH school-aged children vs prospective parents without, as exogenous variation in shadow-education expenditure
return_separated: NO - the exposure is expenditure; the instrument shifts demand composition, not the return to schooling
own_income_held: PARTIAL - province and year FE plus controls, but income is not the instrument's exclusion
effect: a 1% rise in average shadow-education expenditure lowers TFR by 0.18-0.26%; effect MORE pronounced for higher-order births
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS - and it is the only identified estimate on a REALIZED national fertility rate
routing: C.2.f's. Authors frame it as quantity-quality, which is C.3.d's language, but the varying object is required spending to keep pace, not the return.

study: Zhou, Shao & Zhang, The impact of China's 'Double Reduction' policy on the fertility and education investment behaviour of Chinese households
setting: China; CFPS 2018 for the empirical arm, national calibration for the model
design: TWO PARTS. Sec III: IV on CFPS 2018, adults 18-50 with children in compulsory education, n=3,481; OLS/2SLS, Poisson/IV-Poisson, Probit/IV-Probit; instruments = mean shadow-ed spend of pupils one year older and one year younger in the same county. Secs IV-VI: calibrated heterogeneous-agent model with endogenous fertility, urban/rural zhongkao admission, DeepHAM+DIRECT algorithm; the policy result is a SIMULATION
return_separated: NO in the empirical arm; the MODEL is explicitly positional but a model is not an estimate
own_income_held: UNCLEAR - income is a control, but the instrument is county peer spending which is plausibly correlated with county income
outcome: ideal number of children; second-child intention
effect: empirical: shadow-education expenditure has a significant NEGATIVE effect on fertility intentions across all six estimators. Simulated: regulating shadow education 'can boost fertility', rising with regulatory stringency
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS on the empirical arm; the policy result carries no identification
routing: SPLIT, and NEVER pooled with C2F0428 despite the same policy - one is an estimate, one a simulation. RISK OF BIAS: the instrument is county-level peer spending, which IS the reference standard this chapter names as the mechanism, so it plausibly affects intentions directly.

study: Lu, Wei & Fan, Educational competition and reduced family size in China
design: cross-sectional OLS association; exposure = number of private tutoring centres within 800 m of a school as a proxy for competition intensity
own_income_held: PARTIAL - income heterogeneity split, not held
outcome: number of younger siblings of the surveyed student
effect: one or more tutoring centres within 800 m associated with a 0.04-child reduction in younger siblings; strongest among low- and middle-income families
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS in sign, but the authors themselves write 'associated with' and 'may'
routing: NEW CELL added at extraction: the rubric had no context cell for an UNIDENTIFIED required-investment association, only INEQ_ASSOCIATION for inequality exposures. add-a-cell-when-the-rubric-lacks-one. Context, never primary, never pooled.

study: Chen, Sun & Cui, Expansion of shadow education, status externalities, and fertility intentions
design: OLS with mechanism (mediation-style) analysis; no IV, no DID
own_income_held: NO - income is a heterogeneity split
effect: under STATUS EXTERNALITY, shadow-education expansion has a significant negative effect on fertility intentions; stronger among already-parents, socially connected families, low-income and those without pension insurance. Mechanisms: higher education expenditure, less leisure, education anxiety
routing: Names C.2.f's mechanism explicitly (地位外部性 / status externality) - the closest vocabulary match in the pool - but carries no identification.

study: Kim, The Race for Elite Destinations: Education Competition and Low Fertility in Korea
setting: South Korea, calibrated to national data
policy_or_shock: counterfactual: replacing score-based assignment with a capacity-preserving lottery
design: quantitative model calibrated to an ASSIGNMENT EXTERNALITY - when all families spend more the admission bar rises. Not an identified estimate
return_separated: YES conceptually - the model's externality is purely positional, with near-zero measured returns to tutoring
effect: lottery assignment raises completed fertility by 0.24 children per couple; pronatal transfers deliver one eighth of that; education taxes almost none. Families devote 9% of lifetime income to education with near-zero measured returns. CRITICALLY: 'Preference shifts, NOT a fiercer race, explain the decline across cohorts'
sign_vs_c2f: MIXED - the strongest formal statement of C.2.f's mechanism, and its own decomposition attributes the historical cohort decline to preferences rather than to intensifying competition
routing: Context, not an estimate. But its 0.24-children counterfactual and its cohort decomposition are the two most decision-relevant numbers in the pool for the demsig section.

study: Xu & Wu, Income Inequality and the Realization of Fertility Desires in China: Evidence from CGSS Panel Data
design: two-way fixed effects at province and year level
outcome: fertility GAP = ideal minus actual number of children
effect: higher regional income inequality significantly WIDENS the fertility gap, via intensified relative deprivation and lowered perceived socioeconomic status
routing: Conference proceedings, not peer-reviewed journal - weight accordingly at risk of bias.

study: Lee, Widening Regional Economic Disparities and Fertility Decline in South Korea: A Cross-Level Analysis
design: spatial panel with two-way FE (229 districts, 2015-2021) plus multilevel models of married women 19-49 from the 2020 Census; exposure is Yitzhaki's relative deprivation index
outcome: crude birth rate; births per woman
effect: growth in regional disparity has a significant negative effect on crude birth rates; multilevel models confirm regions with sharper inequality increases recorded fewer births per woman
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS in sign; the authors describe them as 'negative associations' and a 'potential mechanism'
routing: Identified only by FE; treat as associational at risk of bias.

study: The impact of income inequality on the fertility intention: a micro perspective based on relative deprivation
design: IV 2SLS on an individual relative-deprivation index, with mechanism analysis
effect: an increase in income inequality BOOSTS fertility intentions, robust to 2SLS. Channels: 'build hopes on children', 'allocate more time to families', and 'PUT LESS VALUE ON CHILDREN'S EDUCATION'. Larger for the poorly educated, low-asset, and those without pension insurance
sign_vs_c2f: RUNS AGAINST - the sign is POSITIVE and the mechanism is the reverse of C.2.f's: inequality lowers the value placed on children's education, reducing rather than raising required investment
routing: Primary cell, opposite sign. Must be in the synthesis, not filtered out.

study: Meng & Xie, Income Inequality, Human Capital Aspirations, and Fertility Decisions / Income Inequality, Educational Aspirations, and Fertility Behavior (VERSION PAIR - ONE STUDY)
design: IV estimation at regional and individual level; educational aspirations as mediator
effect: income inequality significantly AMPLIFIES fertility: individuals in high-disparity regions or with heightened relative deprivation have MORE children. Mediator: higher inequality lowers educational aspirations, which reduces the anticipated cost of children and paradoxically raises fertility
sign_vs_c2f: RUNS AGAINST - positive sign, and the mediator runs opposite to C.2.f's required-investment channel
routing: ONE STUDY, TWO RECORDS (version-pair-is-one-study): same authors, same institution, same CFPS data, near-identical construct counts (relative deprivation 27/32, Gini 27/26, IV 9/10, CFPS 15/15). Count ONCE.

study: Women's relative status and childbearing intentions: empirical evidence from Iran
design: multilevel models of intention to have more children at parities one and two
effect: only a MODEST effect of women's relative status on childbearing intentions at both parities; the authors conclude relative status matters less in low-fertility regimes than in pre-transitional ones
routing: RE-CELLED. 'Relative status of women' here means status relative to MEN, i.e. gender equity - D.2.a's estimand - not position in the income distribution. This is scope section 8 Wall 10's gender homonym arriving in the primary cell, exactly as measured (30 records).

study: Johansson, Status Anxiety and Demographic Contraction of Privileged Populations
design: conceptual and historical essay; no estimation
effect: argues status anxiety among privileged populations drives their demographic contraction; no quantitative estimate
routing: The earliest clear statement of C.2.f's mechanism found in the pool (1987). Context.

study: Young, Education, Care, and Fertility in South Korea: Essays on Household Constraints and Social Pressure
design: Ch2 'Can Parents Overspend...? Peer Effects in Korea's Shadow Education Market' - PSM and AIPW with placebo tests, outcome is SPENDING. Ch3 'Rat Race, Educational Signaling, and Fertility' - a MODEL. Ch4 - numerical care model
return_separated: YES in the Ch3 model (signaling, not returns)
outcome: shadow-education spending (Ch2); fertility in the Ch3 model
effect: Ch2 identifies peer effects in shadow-education spending. Ch3 models a rat race in which educational signaling raises the perceived cost of children and reduces fertility
sign_vs_c2f: SUPPORTS, but no identified FERTILITY estimate
routing: Link 1 only. The identified chapter has no fertility outcome; the fertility chapter is a model.

study: Lee, Exploring ways to revitalize public education and reduce private education costs to increase fertility rate in Korea
design: policy essay and comparative discussion; no estimation
effect: argues that revitalising public education and cutting private education costs would raise Korean fertility; no estimate
